core_principles: Increasing the ankle abduction angle (turning the foot outward) during the lunge exercise increases the muscle activity of the quadriceps femoris.
An ankle abduction angle of 60 degrees is highly effective for selective muscle strengthening of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO).
Strengthening the VMO helps correct muscle imbalances between the vastus lateralis (VL) and VMO, which is key to managing patellofemoral pain syndrome.
Adduction of the hip joint and the tibia during the lunge exercise is beneficial for VMO activation.
Abduction of the femur during the lunge diminishes the force delivered to the lateral patellofemoral joint, thereby decreasing pressure on the knee joint.
common_mistakes: Allowing a muscle imbalance where a weakened vastus medialis oblique (VMO) is overpowered by the vastus lateralis (VL), pulling the patella excessively laterally.
specific_findings: Fifteen male healthy volunteers participated in the study.
All participants performed the lunge exercise with different angles of ankle abduction (0°, 20°, 40°, 60°).
The most significantly increased muscle activity was evident in the vastus medialis oblique (VMO) when the ankle abduction was 60°.
In a previous study, the lunge exercise was shown to activate the muscle activity of VMO by 77% as compared to other exercise schemes

core_principles: To prevent upper body sway during the lunge, look straight ahead and place hands on the waist.

Increasing the ankle abduction angle (turning the foot outward) during a lunge gradually increases the muscle activity of the quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and vastus medialis oblique).
An ankle abduction angle of 60 degrees is highly effective for selective strengthening of the vastus medialis oblique (VMO).
common_mistakes: Allowing the upper body to sway during the movement.
specific_findings: Study analyzed 15 healthy males (mean age: 21.4 ± 3.0 years, mean weight: 71.5 ± 6.8 kg, mean height: 164.1 ± 7.9 cm).
VMO muscle activity increased from 44.2 ± 24.0% at 0° ankle abduction to 63.6 ± 33.8% at 60° ankle abduction (p<0.01).
VL muscle activity increased from 41.3 ± 20.9% at 0° ankle abduction to 57.0 ± 28.7% at 60° ankle abduction (p<0.01).
RF muscle activity increased from 23.0 ± 12.8% at 0° ankle abduction to 37.6 ± 14.5% at 60° ankle abduction (p<0.01).
